newsitem.title: USA: JFK Jr., Peter Lynch odd allies in proposal.
newsitem.headline: JFK Jr., Peter Lynch odd allies in proposal.

text.p: The quest for social security reform has produced an odd couple: mutual funds guru Peter Lynch and John F. Kennedy Jr., the editor of George, the fast-growing monthly political magazine.

Kennedy, son of the late President John F. Kennedy, gives Lynch's call for a two-tier social security system that will allow part of social security taxes to be invested in the stock market prominent play in the latest issue of the magazine, which hit newsstands Friday.
The theme of the issue is what the future will hold and Kennedy, in an interview with Reuters, said most of the magazine's contributors were basically optimistic.
"If we do what Peter says, we may be able to work our way out of it (the social security crisis)."

With social security expected to start running a deficit in 2012, a divided Advisory Council on Social Security this week presented a series of options that included investing public funds in private markets and allowing citizens to set up individual investment accounts.
In his article, "Many Happy Returns," Lynch, who turned Fidelity's Magellan Fund into the country's largest mutual fund, suggests that the best idea would be to have two tiers of benefits.

One tier would be a continuation of the current system financed by 10.4 percent of the 12.4 percent Social Security tax. Lynch said this would provide a safety net for pensioners. The second tier would be an option in which people could invest the remaining 2 percent in a stock market programme or in a supplemental government plan.

"All in all the average citizen would get two boosts from having a portion of the Social Security tax enter the equity worlds. First retirement nest eggs would grow faster. Second more equity capital would increase our nation's productivity," Lynch wrote.

Kennedy said George was interested in tackling the social security issue and "make it accessible to people." The magazine, which began 18 months ago with a circulation of 250,000, now boasts nearly 400,000 readers a month.
Like many new magazines, Kennedy said "George" was still running at a loss but that he was pleased with its progress, especially in drawing advertisers.
"January, February and March are supposed to be lean months for advertising but we are getting between 70 and 80 pages of ads," he said.

"We would like to be quoted more. People are still sniffing us out. There is a certain human inclination to be sceptical. But we are trying to cover politics in a different way," he said, adding that editing George was "great fun."
